title: Why Nikole Hannah-Jones is wrong about failing schools ut-failing-schools/
author: David Harsanyi
summary: David Harsanyi rejects Nikole Hannah-Jones's premise that parents owe their school choices to the collective good, arguing that the first duty to society is to care for one's own children. He recalls low-income Hispanic parents in Denver who could not afford to wait for reforms while their children fell behind, and compares choosing a failing school to shopping at the worst supermarket to improve it for others. Harsanyi disputes her claim that schools serving poor Black students are underfunded, citing P.S. 307's $52,000 per-pupil spending and New York's high costs alongside widespread failure on state tests. He points to Mississippi's literacy gains at far lower spending and faults her essay for never mentioning teachers unions. He also argues that tying schools to residence prices families out of good districts, and concludes that she learned little from the experience.
points: Harsanyi argues there is nothing immoral about prioritizing one's own children in school decisions.
Children in failing schools, he says, have only a few years before they are left behind and cannot wait for reform.
P.S. 307 already had the high spending, small classes, and good pay that reformers on the left recommend.
Mississippi raised elementary reading from 49th to the top ten while spending about $12,000 per student.
Residential school assignment inflates home prices near good schools and keeps many working families out.
quotes: I’m sorry, but the first and best thing you can do for the “collective good” is to take care of yourself and your children.
Students simply didn’t have the luxury of waiting around for reforms that might never materialize, much less participate in fixing schools for the next generation.

No sane person says to themselves, ‘Hey, we should shop at the closest but crappiest supermarket so we can help improve the place for shoppers in the future.’ They choose the one that meets their needs.
PS 307 does all the things that leftists have been imploring us to make schools successful. More money. Smaller class sizes. Good pay.

It has experienced a dramatic rise in national reading and math scores for elementary students over the past decade, rising from 49th in reading to the top 10. It did it by overhauling early literacy education, retraining teachers, and implementing academic accountability.
Many middle- and working-class families are priced out of areas with good schools because of inflated home values directly tied to schools.
Hannah-Jones’s instinct to sacrifice her child’s education speaks of an overpoliticized mind.
